When Ines Farrow cleared her great-aunt Odile’s attic in Carrow last spring, she found a flat tin canister wedged behind the chimney. Inside lay one reel of film; on the lid someone had pencilled “Fair Day, Ferry St.” Her older brother, Colm, who had inherited the house with her, promptly wrote the address of the county archive across the lid in black marker.

Teodor Brask, who owns the Lantern on Ferry Street and keeps its piano as it was in the early years, telephoned Wren Halloway, an archivist in Dunmere, who came the next week. The archivist found the reel sound and supple, though film that old, she said, can catch fire near a hot lamp. When she asked for an empty spool, Brask sent one across the lobby with a gentle underhand pitch. Colm, holding a frame to the window, was the first to recognize the street and place it in town: their grandfather’s hardware sign hung over a doorway.

The archive’s laboratory had a waiting list, and the delay stretched through the summer while a collector in the city wrote twice offering to buy it. The archive paid for the copy out of its own money, so Brask had only the waiting to bear.

Brask wanted live music, and the only person in Carrow who had ever played for silent films was Mabel Quill, the Lantern’s old pianist. She had not set foot in the building in forty years. Ines and Colm argued with Brask that a recording would do, but he called at Mabel’s house three evenings running, and on the fourth she came down and asked him to run the copy for her privately while she found the music.

In October the copy was screened at the Lantern to a full house, and the reel showed the town exactly what the pencilled lid had promised. The original stayed in Dunmere, where everyone agreed it belonged. Afterward, Brask asked Mabel whether she would play for the next showing. She told him she would, as long as the original reel stayed locked in the archive’s vault and was never carried into the Lantern’s hot little booth.
